American jewelry had a good first half — on paper. Revenue rose 8.6% over six months and 13% in June.

But the honest number is the one on the tag: the average purchase price climbed about 19%. The growth is coming from bigger purchases by fewer hands. Tennis bracelets (+14%) and pearls carried it. Naturals sold fewer units at higher prices; lab-grown sold more units at flat prices.

A market that grows by selling dearer goods to fewer people rewards the specialist counter — and squeezes the value end. Link in bio.

A diamond mine doesn't go dark the day the last truck leaves the pit.

Rio Tinto closed Diavik — its last diamond asset — in March. Yet in the second quarter it still recovered 33,000 carats from the remaining ore. Output fell 97% year on year, and first-half production came to 1.1 million carats, down 51%.

Those last certified Canadian carats reach a market short of exactly that story: closures worldwide are quietly rebuilding the scarcity case for natural stones. Rio sells its final production through year-end. Link in bio.

When gold reads as value, shoppers buy the metal and skip the markup.

Chow Tai Fook, Greater China's largest chain, posted quarterly retail sales up 15.1% — and up 44.8% in Hong Kong and Macau. The engine was weight-based gold jewelry, sold by the gram: same-store sales there leapt 63.7%, and 38% on the mainland, as softer gold after June's dip pulled buyers in. Design-led, fixed-price pieces slipped about 1%.

It's a region, not one chain: Luk Fook rose 32% and Chow Sang Sang 16%. A metal story wearing a retail costume — and metal stories turn. Link in bio.
